title: Distributed Systems
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 400-level Distributed Systems curriculum (Tanenbaum/Coulouris-style) covering architectural models, RPC/middleware, clock synchronization, mutual exclusion, election algorithms, distributed transactions, CAP theorem, consistency/replication, fault tolerance, consensus, naming, deadlock, and distributed data processing.

questions.question: A distributed system is best defined as:
options: A collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system
A single powerful mainframe computer serving multiple terminals
A network of computers that never communicate with each other
A standalone application running on one machine
questions.correct_answer: A collection of independent computers that appears to its users as a single coherent system
questions.explanation: This is the classic Tanenbaum definition distinguishing distributed systems from centralized ones.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a key characteristic of distributed systems?
options: Guaranteed synchronous communication with zero delay
questions.correct_answer: Guaranteed synchronous communication with zero delay
questions.explanation: Real distributed systems have variable network delays; there is no guarantee of instantaneous synchronous communication.

questions.question: In distributed systems terminology, "transparency" refers to:
options: Hiding the details of distribution from users and application programmers
Making all source code publicly visible
Displaying network topology to end users
questions.correct_answer: Hiding the details of distribution from users and application programmers
questions.explanation: Transparency means the distributed nature of the system is concealed so it appears as a single system.

questions.question: Which type of transparency ensures that users cannot tell whether a resource has moved to another location?
questions.correct_answer: Migration transparency
questions.explanation: Migration transparency hides the fact that a resource may move from one location to another.

questions.question: Which architectural model involves a client sending a request to a server and waiting for a response?
questions.correct_answer: Client-server model
questions.explanation: The client-server model is the classic request-reply interaction pattern.

questions.question: In peer-to-peer architecture, which statement is true?
options: All nodes play similar roles and can act as both client and server
Only one node can provide services to all others
A central server must approve all communications
Nodes cannot communicate directly with each other
questions.correct_answer: All nodes play similar roles and can act as both client and server
questions.explanation: In P2P systems, each node (peer) can both consume and provide services, without a strict client/server distinction.

questions.question: Remote Procedure Call (RPC) allows a program to:
options: Call a procedure located on a remote machine as if it were local
Transfer files between two disks on the same machine
questions.correct_answer: Call a procedure located on a remote machine as if it were local
questions.explanation: RPC is a communication paradigm that abstracts network calls to look like local procedure calls.

questions.question: In RPC, the client-side stub is responsible for:
options: Marshalling parameters and sending the request to the server
questions.correct_answer: Marshalling parameters and sending the request to the server
questions.explanation: The client stub packages (marshals) arguments into a message format and forwards it over the network.

questions.question: Marshalling in distributed systems refers to:
options: Converting data structures into a format suitable for transmission over a network
questions.correct_answer: Converting data structures into a format suitable for transmission over a network
questions.explanation: Marshalling (or serialization) packs parameters/data into a byte stream for network transfer.

questions.question: Which of these best describes middleware in a distributed system?
options: Software layer that provides common services and abstractions to applications across a network
A hardware component that routes packets
An operating system kernel module only
questions.correct_answer: Software layer that provides common services and abstractions to applications across a network
questions.explanation: Middleware sits between the OS/network and applications, providing services like communication, naming, and coordination.

questions.question: Because distributed systems lack a single global clock, which mechanism is commonly used to order events?
options: A single centralized wall clock shared by all nodes
questions.correct_answer: Lamport logical clocks
questions.explanation: Lamport timestamps provide a logical ordering of events without relying on synchronized physical clocks.

questions.question: Lamport's "happened-before" relation is used to:
options: Establish a partial ordering of events in a distributed system
questions.correct_answer: Establish a partial ordering of events in a distributed system
questions.explanation: The happened-before relation captures causal dependencies between events across processes.

questions.question: Vector clocks improve upon Lamport clocks primarily by:
options: Allowing detection of causal relationships and concurrency between events
Eliminating the need for any clock at all
Reducing the number of processes needed
questions.correct_answer: Allowing detection of causal relationships and concurrency between events
questions.explanation: Unlike scalar Lamport timestamps, vector clocks can determine whether two events are causally related or concurrent.

questions.question: Cristian's algorithm is used for:
options: Synchronizing a client's clock with a time server over a network
questions.correct_answer: Synchronizing a client's clock with a time server over a network
questions.explanation: Cristian's algorithm estimates round-trip delay to adjust a client's clock to match a time server.

questions.question: The Berkeley algorithm for clock synchronization differs from Cristian's algorithm because it:
options: Uses an internal coordinator that averages clock readings from a group of machines without an accurate external time source
Requires every node to have a GPS receiver
Only works on a single machine
questions.correct_answer: Uses an internal coordinator that averages clock readings from a group of machines without an accurate external time source
questions.explanation: Berkeley's algorithm computes an average time from participating machines rather than syncing to an external authoritative clock.

questions.question: Which algorithm is commonly used for achieving mutual exclusion in a distributed system without a central coordinator?
questions.correct_answer: Ricart-Agrawala algorithm
questions.explanation: The Ricart-Agrawala algorithm is a permission-based distributed mutual exclusion algorithm using timestamped requests.

questions.question: In the token ring approach to distributed mutual exclusion, a process may enter its critical section when:
options: It possesses the token that is passed around the logical ring
It has the lowest process ID
It receives permission from all other processes individually
The coordinator explicitly restarts the ring
questions.correct_answer: It possesses the token that is passed around the logical ring
questions.explanation: Only the process holding the circulating token is allowed to access the critical section.

questions.question: The Bully algorithm is used for:
options: Electing a coordinator process among a group of distributed processes
questions.correct_answer: Electing a coordinator process among a group of distributed processes
questions.explanation: In the Bully algorithm, the process with the highest ID takes over as coordinator when the current one fails.

questions.question: In the Ring election algorithm, election messages are:
options: Passed around a logical ring, with each process adding its ID until the highest is elected
Sent only to the current coordinator
Never used because rings do not support elections
questions.correct_answer: Passed around a logical ring, with each process adding its ID until the highest is elected
questions.explanation: Each process forwards the election message, appending its own ID, until the highest ID circulates back and is declared coordinator.

questions.question: The Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol is designed to ensure:
options: Atomicity of a distributed transaction across multiple participants
questions.correct_answer: Atomicity of a distributed transaction across multiple participants
questions.explanation: 2PC ensures all participants either commit or abort a transaction together, preserving atomicity.

questions.question: In 2PC, the phase where the coordinator asks all participants if they are ready to commit is called:
questions.correct_answer: The voting (prepare) phase
questions.explanation: In the first phase, the coordinator polls participants for their vote to commit or abort.

questions.question: A major drawback of the Two-Phase Commit protocol is that it:
options: Can block indefinitely if the coordinator fails after the voting phase
Works only with a single participant
questions.correct_answer: Can block indefinitely if the coordinator fails after the voting phase
questions.explanation: 2PC is a blocking protocol; participants may wait indefinitely for the coordinator's decision if it crashes.

questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, a distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee at most:
options: Two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
All three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
questions.correct_answer: Two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
questions.explanation: CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a system must trade off between consistency and availability.

questions.question: Which replication consistency model requires that all replicas reflect updates immediately, appearing as a single copy?
questions.correct_answer: Strict/strong consistency
questions.explanation: Strong consistency guarantees that any read returns the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data.

questions.question: Eventual consistency guarantees that:
options: If no new updates occur, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value
All replicas are always identical at every instant
Updates are never propagated to other replicas
questions.correct_answer: If no new updates occur, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence but guarantees convergence over time absent further writes.

questions.question: Which fault-tolerance approach involves running multiple redundant copies of a service so that failure of one does not stop the system?
questions.correct_answer: Replication
questions.explanation: Replication maintains multiple copies of data or services to tolerate failures.

questions.question: A distributed consensus algorithm such as Paxos or Raft is primarily used to:
options: Get a group of distributed nodes to agree on a single value despite failures
questions.correct_answer: Get a group of distributed nodes to agree on a single value despite failures
questions.explanation: Consensus algorithms ensure that non-faulty nodes in a distributed system agree on the same value, even amid crashes or delays.

questions.question: In the Raft consensus algorithm, at any given time a node can be in one of these states EXCEPT:
questions.correct_answer: Broker
questions.explanation: Raft defines three node states -- leader, follower, and candidate -- but not "broker", which is a messaging-system concept.

questions.question: The Domain Name System (DNS) is an example of a distributed:
questions.correct_answer: Naming service
questions.explanation: DNS maps human-readable domain names to IP addresses in a distributed, hierarchical naming system.

questions.question: Distributed deadlock detection typically involves constructing a:
questions.correct_answer: Wait-for graph across multiple nodes
questions.explanation: A distributed wait-for graph tracks which processes are waiting for resources held by others, and a cycle indicates deadlock.

questions.question: The Google MapReduce model processes large datasets by:
options: Splitting work into a Map phase and a Reduce phase distributed across many machines
Running everything on a single powerful machine
Eliminating the need for any data partitioning
questions.correct_answer: Splitting work into a Map phase and a Reduce phase distributed across many machines
questions.explanation: MapReduce distributes computation as parallel map tasks followed by aggregation/reduce tasks across a cluster.

questions.question: A microservices architecture structures an application as:
options: A collection of small, independently deployable services communicating over a network
One large database shared with no APIs
questions.correct_answer: A collection of small, independently deployable services communicating over a network
questions.explanation: Microservices decompose an application into loosely coupled, independently deployable services.

questions.question: Which of these is a common message-oriented middleware technology used in distributed systems?
questions.correct_answer: Apache Kafka
questions.explanation: Apache Kafka is a distributed publish-subscribe messaging platform widely used for asynchronous communication between services.

questions.question: Load balancing in a distributed system primarily aims to:
options: Distribute incoming requests evenly across multiple servers to avoid overload
Reduce the number of servers to one
Increase the physical distance between servers
questions.correct_answer: Distribute incoming requests evenly across multiple servers to avoid overload
questions.explanation: Load balancers spread client requests across a pool of servers to optimize resource use and prevent bottlenecks.
